title: Colours, Logos and Branding
subtitle: How to talk about the look of a brand
description: Learn simple words to talk about how a brand looks — its colours, logo, and style — and why it matters for marketing.
dialogueSubtitle: Riley shows Dana the Brightline brand and explains the choices

vocabulary.definition: A small picture or symbol that stands for a company or brand.
vocabulary.example: The Brightline logo is a blue circle with the company name.

vocabulary.definition: What you see when light hits something. For example: red, blue, or green.
vocabulary.example: We use blue and white as our main colours.

vocabulary.definition: The way something looks — its colours, shapes, and style.
vocabulary.example: The design of our website uses clean lines and bright colours.

vocabulary.definition: The name and look of a company or product.
vocabulary.example: A strong brand helps people remember who you are.
We use strong images on our website to show what the brand looks like.

vocabulary.definition: The style of writing used in text.
vocabulary.example: We use the same font on all our marketing materials so everything looks the same.

vocabulary.definition: The way something looks or feels.
vocabulary.example: Our brand style is clean and modern.

vocabulary.definition: The look and feel that makes a brand easy to know.
vocabulary.example: A strong brand identity helps people remember who you are and what you stand for.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Say what a symbol, colour, or logo means for a brand.
phrasalVerbs.example: Our blue colour stands for trust and calm.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Be easy to see and remember — different from others.
phrasalVerbs.example: Our logo is simple so it stands out on any background.
We use colours and fonts that fit with the style of the brand.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Say how something appears to people.
phrasalVerbs.example: The website should look like the rest of our brand — clean, blue, and modern.

phrasalVerbs.definition: The feeling or idea that people get when they see your brand.
phrasalVerbs.example: We want the brand to come across as friendly and easy to trust.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Create a strong look and name that people know and remember.
phrasalVerbs.example: It takes time to build a brand, but it is worth it.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Dana, let me show you the Brightline [[brand:the name and look of a company or product]]. We just updated it last year.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: I like the [[logo:a small picture or symbol that stands for a company or brand]]. It is simple and easy to remember.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Thank you — we wanted something that stands out. The [[design:the way something looks — its colours, shapes, and style]] is clean and modern. Simple always works best.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Why did you choose blue as your main [[colour:what you see when light hits something]]?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Blue stands for trust and calm — and that is what we want our brand to come across as. It fits with our [[style:the way something looks or feels]] too.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: And what about the [[font:the style of writing used in text]]?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: We use the same font on everything — the website, emails, leaflets. It keeps the brand identity consistent and easy to know.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: What about [[image:a picture or photo]]s? How do you choose them?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: We only use images that look like our brand — clean, bright, and with real people. No stock photos that look too old or too formal.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: How long did it take to build a strong brand [[identity:the look and feel that makes a brand easy to know]]?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: About two years! We tried a lot of different things before we found what worked. But it is worth it — people now know who we are straight away.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: I need to work on the identity for my agency. Maybe I can take some ideas from Brightline!

chooseResponse.instructions: Work in groups. Read the question. Talk about which answer (A, B, or C) is best. Choose together, then click to check.

items.customerLine: Why is your logo so simple?
options: We wanted it to be easy to remember and to stand out on any background. Simple logos work best — people can see them clearly on a screen, a card, or a poster.
Simple logos are cheaper to make.
items.explanation: B is correct. It gives a real reason — easy to remember, stands out — and says where it needs to work. A gives no reason. C sounds like money was the only reason, which is not a good message for a brand.

items.customerLine: Why did you choose those colours?
options: We liked the way they look together.
Blue stands for trust and calm — those are the feelings we want people to have when they see our brand. White keeps it clean and easy to read.
Colours are mostly personal choice in branding.
items.explanation: B is correct. It says what each colour means and connects it to the brand. A sounds like it was just a personal choice. C gives no real reason and makes colour choices sound unimportant.

items.customerLine: How do you keep your brand looking the same everywhere?
options: We try to use the same things as much as possible.
We use the same logo, colours, font, and style on everything — the website, emails, leaflets, and social media. It keeps the brand identity clear and easy to know.
We have guidelines but people do not always follow them.
items.explanation: B is correct. It names what is kept the same — logo, colours, font, style — and says where it appears. A is too vague. C sounds like the brand is not consistent, which is not a good message.

items.customerLine: Does branding really matter for a small company?
options: Yes — a strong brand identity helps people remember who you are, even if you are small. It makes you look more professional and easy to trust.
It helps, but it is not the most important thing.
Big companies need it more than small ones.
items.explanation: A is correct. It says clearly that branding matters and gives two good reasons — people remember you and you look more professional. B sounds unsure. C says small companies do not need good branding, which is not true.

profileMatch.instructions: You are Riley. Three companies want help with their brand. As a group, talk about which part of branding to focus on first for each company. Click 'Check Matches' when you agree.

profiles.name: A new company with no brand yet
profiles.description: A new small business just started. They have a name but no logo, no colours, and no style. They do not know where to start.

profiles.name: A company with a good logo but inconsistent look
profiles.description: A company has a logo they like, but their website, emails, and social media all look different. Clients find it hard to know it is the same company.

profiles.name: A company with a strong visual brand but a bad image
profiles.description: A company has a great logo and colours, but the photos they use on their website and social media are old and formal. It does not fit with their style.

options.label: Start with the logo
options.description: Design a simple logo first — one that is easy to remember and stands out. The logo will become the base for all other brand choices, like colours and fonts.

options.label: Make it consistent
options.description: Use the same logo, colours, and font on everything — website, emails, and social media. A consistent brand identity helps people know it is the same company everywhere.

options.label: Update the images
options.description: Choose new photos that fit with the brand style — clean, bright, and with real people. Images are often the first thing people see, so they need to look right.

finishTheLine.instructions: The marketer's line is not finished. As a group, talk about how you would finish it. Use words from this lesson. There is no one right answer — share your ideas, then click to see one example.

items.customerLine: Why does branding matter in marketing?
items.salespersonStart: Branding matters because it helps people remember you. A strong brand
items.suggestedCompletion: identity — your logo, colours, and style — makes your company easy to know. When people see your design, they should know straight away who you are.

items.customerLine: How do you choose colours for a brand?
items.salespersonStart: Think about what feeling you want people to have when they see your brand. Each colour
items.suggestedCompletion: stands for something different. Blue stands for trust. Green stands for nature or health. Red stands for energy. Choose colours that fit with what your brand is about.

items.salespersonStart: A good logo is simple and easy to remember. It should
items.suggestedCompletion: stand out and look good on any background — a website, a business card, or a poster. The best logos are ones that people see once and remember for a long time.

items.customerLine: How long does it take to build a strong brand identity?
items.salespersonStart: It takes time — usually at least one or two years. You have to try different things and
items.suggestedCompletion: see what people like. The key is to keep the design consistent — use the same logo, font, and colours everywhere so people start to know and trust the brand.
